label: Current Oil Price ($/barrel)
description: Brent crude benchmark price as of 23 August 2026. Observed path: pre-war ~$70–83; March peak prints of $118–$139; $71.57 on 1 July as the MoU briefly de-risked the market; $100.69 on 23 July during the 13-night campaign; $91.62 settle on 19 August (WTI $85.83). The panic premium of March is gone; a structural Hormuz premium remains. Paper-physical dislocation is smaller than in March because Gulf producers have rerouted some barrels (Saudi East-West pipeline, Fujairah STS) and because demand destruction plus SPR releases filled the first months. The default distribution is now centered near $92, not $120.

source.citation: Reuters 'Oil prices settle near 4-week high' 19 August 2026 (Brent $91.62, WTI $85.83); Wikipedia energy section (Brent $71.57 on 1 July, $100.69 on 23 July); Reuters 'Oil market starts pricing in a prolonged Hormuz crisis' 18 August 2026

label: Strait of Hormuz Closure Status
description: Current operational status of the Strait of Hormuz for commercial shipping. Observed as of 23 August 2026: not fully open and not a literal zero. Pre-war throughput was ~130 vessels/day and ~18 million bpd. Kpler counted ~13 crossings/day in mid-August and 7 on 21 August, the lowest daily print of the war. Trump says the strait is 'open and operating' and 'all water mines have been removed'; Ghalibaf says it stays shut until US conditions are met. The accurate state is closed_selective_passage — a handful of hulls (some dark, some on the UN/Omani southern route, occasional Iraqi tankers Iran allows as a concession that preserves Iranian management claims) against a collapsed commercial baseline.

source.citation: Kpler / Reuters Hormuz crossing counts 13–21 August 2026 (7–13/day vs ~130 pre-war); Forbes 18 August 2026 (Ghalibaf); Crisis Group trigger list 18 August 2026 (Trump 'open and operating'); Lloyd's List

label: Global Oil Production Loss
description: Net reduction in global oil supply reaching market due to the conflict. The March 'over 10 million bpd' emergency print is no longer the whole story. Kpler: Hormuz crude+products averaged 4.8 million bpd in July and ~2 million bpd so far in August, versus ~18 million bpd pre-war — a 13–16 million bpd hole through the strait — but substitution is real. Saudi East-West pipeline and Fujairah ship-to-ship transfers, plus demand destruction and SPR barrels, mean the net market shortfall is smaller than the strait hole. UAE crude exports in August were actually slightly above 2025. The modal bin therefore moves from over_10m_bpd toward 7_10m_bpd, with a fat tail still in over_10m if ADNOC-linked attacks and Economic D-Day collapse the workarounds.

source.citation: Reuters / Kpler 18 August 2026 (Hormuz 4.8 mb/d July, ~2 mb/d August vs 18 mb/d pre-war; UAE August exports 3.38 mb/d); IEA Oil Market Report; EIA

label: GCC Food Security Crisis
description: Severity of food security disruption in Gulf Cooperation Council states. GCC countries import 80-90% of their food, primarily through ports now affected by Hormuz closure and regional shipping disruptions. Observed: GCC food imports disrupted by approximately 70% as of late March, with consumer food prices up 40-120% depending on category. UAE and Saudi have activated strategic grain reserves (60-90 day supply). Qatar is worst affected due to single-point-of-entry vulnerability. Emergency airlifts of essential goods have begun.

source.citation: FAO 'Gulf Region Food Security Emergency Assessment' March 2026; GCC food reserve status reports; Reuters 'GCC food imports disrupted 70%' March 22, 2026; WFP emergency brief on Gulf food supply chains

label: Shipping Insurance Market Status
description: Status of the war-risk insurance market for commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, and Arabian Sea. Observed: the market is effectively frozen for Gulf transits. Lloyd's and the International Group of P&I Clubs have designated the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Oman as excluded war-risk zones. Premiums for any remaining coverage have risen to 5-10% of hull value per transit (vs. 0.01% pre-conflict). Most shipowners cannot obtain coverage at any price, halting commercial transits entirely.

source.citation: Lloyd's Market Association Joint War Committee circulars March 2026; International Group of P&I Clubs exclusion notices; S&P Global 'War risk premiums make Gulf transit uneconomic' March 2026; Hellenic Shipping News

label: Hormuz Reopening Timeline
description: Projected timeline for resumption of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, measured from 23 August 2026. The April Dallas Fed / Baker Hughes consensus that the strait would not fully reopen until H2 2026 is now a miss — August is H2 and daily crossings are in the single digits. The 17 June MoU was supposed to reopen the strait toll-free for 60 days; Iran re-closed it on 20 June over Lebanon, and the window lapsed on 17 August. A 4 August Iran–Oman dual-lane framework (zero tolls, 30-day mine clearance) never started. Ghalibaf's 18 August conditions — lift the blockade, release frozen assets, remove oil sanctions — are a negotiated outcome, not a minesweeping problem. 'Indefinite' is now the modal bin.

source.citation: Kpler '60 days of a broken US-Iran MoU' 19 August 2026; Forbes 18 August 2026; Dallas Fed Energy survey April 2026 (H2 reopen call, now missed); CENTCOM MCM reporting

label: Oil Price 6-Month Forward Trajectory ($/barrel)
description: Projected Brent crude price 6 months forward from 23 August 2026 (approximately February 2027). The March default centered at $140 assumed the panic premium would persist. It did not: the market learned to live with a half-closed strait, and Brent spent early July in the $70s before repricing the MoU collapse back into the $90s. The forward question is whether Economic D-Day, ADNOC-tanker attacks, and a 1.8 mb/d Q3 deficit (IEA August revision) push prices back to three digits, or whether substitution and demand destruction cap them near $90–110. The default is now centered near $98, not $140.

source.citation: Reuters 18–19 August 2026; IEA August 2026 Oil Market Report (Q3 deficit revised to 1.8 mb/d); ICE Brent; Goldman Sachs Gulf-disruption scenarios

label: Global GDP Impact
description: Estimated impact on global GDP growth from the conflict and energy supply disruption. IEA has warned this is the 'greatest global energy security challenge in history.' Historical analogues: 1973 oil embargo caused ~3% global GDP contraction; 1979 Iranian revolution contributed to 1980-82 recession. Current shock is larger in absolute terms (10M+ bpd vs. 4.3 Mb/d in 1973) but the global economy is less oil-intensive per unit of GDP. IMF and World Bank models suggest 1-2% global GDP reduction per $30/bbl sustained oil price increase.

source.citation: IEA 'greatest global energy security challenge in history' statement March 2026; IMF 'Oil Price Shocks and Global Growth' WP/24/52; World Bank commodity shock modeling; Hamilton (2003) 'What is an oil shock?'; Blanchard-Gali (2010) oil-macro transmission

label: US Inflation Impact
description: Projected US CPI inflation rate over the next 12 months factoring in energy price pass-through. Pre-conflict US inflation was running ~2.5-2.8%. Forecast: >3% based on gasoline price transmission alone. Energy accounts for ~7% of CPI directly but has larger indirect effects through transportation, manufacturing, and food costs. US gasoline prices have risen from ~$3.20/gal to ~$4.50/gal, with further increases likely. The Fed faces a painful dilemma: rate cuts risk inflation spiral, rate holds risk recession deepening.

source.citation: BLS CPI data through February 2026; Fed FOMC minutes March 2026; Goldman Sachs 'US Inflation Under Oil Shock Scenarios' March 2026; historical pass-through estimates: ~2-4% CPI increase per $30/bbl sustained oil price rise (Kilian 2008)

label: US War Cost Estimate
description: Projected total direct US military cost of operations. The air campaign alone is estimated at $2-5 billion per week based on munitions expenditure (TLAMs at $2M each, JDAMs at $25K, B-2 sortie costs), carrier operations ($6.5M/day per CSG), deployed force sustainment, and intelligence/surveillance. If sustained for 3+ months, total costs could approach OIF-scale spending. Excludes indirect costs (VA healthcare, economic losses, interest on debt financing).

source.citation: CBO 'Estimated Costs of US Military Operations Against Iran' rapid assessment March 2026; CRS 'Costs of Major US Wars' historical baseline; DoD comptroller munitions expenditure rates; Stimson Center cost projections

label: Iranian Economic Collapse
description: Severity of Iran's economic collapse as of 23 August 2026. Reuters/Kpler: Iranian crude exports have fallen to 294,000 bpd this month from 1.7 million bpd in 2025. ISNA: inflation exceeded 80% year-on-year in July. The US blockade, reimposed 15 July, and the 20 August 'Economic D-Day' threat (secondary sanctions on any country trading with Iran) are the current squeeze, not just strike damage. The regime is not a failed state: it signed a presidential MoU in June, the SNSC still issues Hormuz conditions, and parliament still legislates. That is 'near_total' economic pain with a functioning wartime state, not 'failed_state.'

source.citation: Reuters 18 August 2026 (exports 294k bpd vs 1.7 mb/d; inflation >80% YoY July per ISNA); Wikipedia 'Economic D-Day' 20 August 2026; World Bank Iran Economic Monitor

label: Energy Market Substitution
description: Speed and effectiveness of global energy market adaptation to Gulf supply loss. Key substitution channels: (1) US SPR release (~350M barrels available, drawdown rate ~4.4 Mb/d max); (2) IEA coordinated emergency stocks (1.2B barrels total member reserves); (3) Saudi East-West Pipeline (5 Mb/d to Yanbu on Red Sea, partially activated); (4) ADNOC Habshan-Fujairah pipeline (1.5 Mb/d bypassing Hormuz); (5) Russian/Kazakh/Nigerian production increases; (6) demand destruction. Combined, these can offset ~5-7 Mb/d, leaving a 3-5 Mb/d structural gap.

source.citation: IEA Emergency Response Review 2025; US DOE SPR operational readiness assessment; Saudi Aramco East-West Pipeline capacity data; ADNOC Habshan-Fujairah pipeline status; EIA 'Global Oil Supply Substitution Analysis' March 2026

label: Global Supply Chain Disruption
description: Severity of cascading supply chain disruptions beyond the energy sector. Observed: severe and worsening as of March 29. Container shipping rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope (already underway from Houthi Red Sea attacks since 2024) has intensified. Petrochemical feedstock shortages are hitting manufacturing in Asia. Gulf-based aluminum, fertilizer, and plastics production is halted. Automotive manufacturers report parts shortages. Air cargo rates from Asia to Europe up 300%. Port congestion at alternative routing hubs (Jebel Ali via overland, Salalah, Mumbai).

source.citation: Drewry Container Shipping Index March 2026; Freightos Baltic Index; WTO 'Trade Disruption Assessment' March 2026; McKinsey Global Supply Chain Pulse March 2026; observed port congestion data from Marine Traffic
